feedback: If the learner predicted the cork rides to the far end: watch again closely — the cork bobs up and down and ends up near where it started, even though wave after wave passes under it. What crossed the tray was the wave pattern (energy), not the water itself.

If the learner says the water travelled across: a single bit of water moves round in a small loop (up and down and a little back and forth) and stays roughly in place; the pattern moves across, the water does not travel with it.
Reinforce correct observation: the cork stayed roughly put and bobbed — so the wave carries energy, not matter, across the tray.
activities.intendedInsight: A wave transfers energy through a medium without carrying the matter along: the cork bobs up and down roughly in place while the wave pattern sweeps on through it.
learnerActions: Float a cork or bottle-top on one end of a tray of water.
Before making any waves, predict in writing or speech: will the cork travel to the far end with the waves, or do something else — and why?
Make waves from one end and watch the cork carefully as several waves pass under it.
Describe what actually crossed the tray: did the water (and cork) travel across, or did the cork stay roughly in place and bob up and down?
Repeat with a bigger disturbance and note whether the cork is now carried across or just bobs more strongly in roughly the same place.
activities.title: Does the cork ride the wave? (water-tray investigation)

feedback: If the learner thinks the ribbon travels along the coil: it returns to roughly its own spot — only the pulse travels the length, showing matter stays put while the wave (energy) moves.

If the learner predicts the big pulse arrives first: on the same slinky the big and small pulses reach the far end at about the same time; amplitude carries more energy, not more speed. Wave speed is set by the medium, not the size of the wave.

For the stadium/domino analogy: no single person travels round the stadium and no single domino moves along the row — each only moves and nudges its neighbour, so what travels round is the wave (energy), not the people or dominoes.
activities.intendedInsight: Energy is passed neighbour-to-neighbour while each part of the medium stays roughly in place; for ordinary-sized pulses, the size of a pulse makes little or no difference to how fast it travels along a given medium.
learnerActions: Lay a slinky or long rope on the floor and send a single pulse from one end to the other; watch the far end react.
Tie a ribbon or marker near the middle of the coil and watch what the ribbon does as the pulse passes it.
Describe what the ribbon does (oscillates and returns to roughly its own spot) versus what the pulse does (travels the length).
Send a big pulse and a small pulse and compare how fast each reaches the far end.
Act out or describe a stadium 'Mexican wave' or a line of falling dominoes, then say which individuals actually travel round/along and which only pass the motion to their neighbour.
activities.title: Pass it along: slinky, rope, and the stadium wave

feedback: If amplitude is marked as the peak-to-peak distance: that distance is the wavelength; amplitude is the height from the middle line up to a peak.
If wavelength is marked as the height: that height is the amplitude; wavelength is measured from one peak across to the next peak.
When both are labelled correctly and the two 'change one at a time' drawings differ as expected, confirm: the learner has separated how tall a wave is from how long it is.
activities.intendedInsight: Amplitude and wavelength are two separate, independent features of a wave: amplitude is the height (linked to energy), wavelength is the peak-to-peak distance.
learnerActions: Draw (or be given) a transverse waveform and mark the crest (highest point) and trough (lowest point).
Mark amplitude as the height from the middle line to a peak, and label it 'how big / how much energy'.
Mark wavelength as the distance from one peak to the next peak, and label it 'how long'.
State in your own words the difference between amplitude (how tall) and wavelength (how long).
Draw a second wave with the same wavelength but larger amplitude, and a third with the same amplitude but longer wavelength, to show the two quantities change independently.
activities.title: Label the wave: amplitude vs wavelength

feedback: If the learner attributes the bigger push to higher speed: recall the slinky — big and small pulses travelled at the same speed. The bigger push comes from more energy (larger amplitude), not greater speed.
Reinforce the sound link: just as a louder note is a bigger vibration, a bigger water wave is a bigger disturbance carrying more energy.
Confirm correct reasoning: bigger amplitude = more energy = bigger effect on the floating object, with speed set by the medium.
activities.intendedInsight: Larger amplitude means more energy, which does more work on objects (a bigger push), but it does not make the wave travel faster.
learnerActions: Float a small object (toy boat, bottle-top) on a water tray and make a small-amplitude wave, noting how much the object is pushed or bobs.
Make a bigger-amplitude wave (same medium) and compare how much the object is pushed or bobs now.
State the relationship: a bigger-amplitude wave carries more energy and moves the object more.
Connect to sound: louder sound comes from a bigger vibration (bigger amplitude), just as a bigger water wave is a bigger disturbance carrying more energy.
Decide and explain whether a bigger wave moves the object more because it travels faster or because it carries more energy — and justify using the slinky same-speed result.
activities.title: Bigger wave, bigger push: amplitude and energy

feedback: If the learner expects the cork to ride to the far side: the model shows it bobbing in place and left behind — the pattern travels, the cork does not.
When amplitude is raised and the push grows but the crossing time does not shorten, confirm: amplitude sets energy/push, not speed.
If amplitude and wavelength are confused on the labels, point to which control changed height versus peak spacing.
activities.intendedInsight: Amplitude and wavelength can be varied independently, and a wave carries energy (which can push objects) without carrying the floating object along with it.
learnerActions: Use a side-on model of a rope or water wave with two separate controls: one that raises the amplitude (a taller wave) and one that stretches the wavelength (peaks further apart), with the terms shown live on the crest and trough as they change.
Predict where a floating cork on the surface will end up, then send a wave across and watch: the cork bobs straight up and down and is left near its starting point while the pattern sweeps through.
Increase the amplitude and observe the same cork bob higher and a floating boat rock and bob more strongly, while both still stay near their starting points — bigger wave, more energy, bigger effect.
Compare a tall wave and a short wave sent across and note whether changing amplitude changed how fast the wave crossed.
activities.title: Optional: side-on wave model with amplitude and wavelength controls

feedback: If the learner says the duck is carried to the far bank: revisit the cork/slinky evidence — for a standard repeating wave the medium bobs in place while energy crosses.

If waves are ordered by wavelength instead of amplitude when ranking energy: for these same-wavelength waves, the difference in energy comes from amplitude (height), so compare heights, not peak spacing.
If the learner reads the curve as the route the water follows: the curve is a graph of displacement; a marked particle actually moves up and down (or back and forth), not along the wavy line.
Confirm a full response: duck bobs in place, energy crosses, amplitude is distinguished from wavelength, and amplitude does not set speed.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates the vocabulary (amplitude, wavelength, crest, trough), the energy-from-amplitude ordering, and the energy-not-matter threshold idea, including why a drawn sine curve is a displacement graph rather than a travel path.
learnerActions: Label amplitude, wavelength, crest and trough on a given waveform.
Answer: as a standard, repeating wave crosses a pond toward the far bank, does a floating duck get carried to the bank, or bob in place? Justify the answer.
Order several drawn waves that have the same wavelength (in the same medium) by the energy they carry, using their amplitudes.
Explain, using a marked particle, why the drawn wavy curve is NOT the path the water or duck physically travels.
Write one or two sentences summarising what a wave carries across (energy) versus what stays behind (the matter/medium).
activities.title: Check and consolidate the wave model
